stem:
A 27-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (PMOS), diagnosed three years ago, attends for review. She has irregular periods and central weight gain, and her BMI is in the obese range. Dark, velvety skin is noted at the back of her neck. She asks what she should be watching out for in her long-term health.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: She is mainly at risk of early menopause, so should have regular bone-density scans and hormone testing
options.B: She is at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, so advise lifestyle change and glucose checks
options.C: She is at risk of type 1 diabetes, so islet autoantibody testing should be arranged now
options.D: She has a high ovarian cancer risk, so should have regular CA-125 and pelvic scanning
options.E: Her long-term risks are no higher than average, so no monitoring is needed after diagnosis

correct_answer: B. She is at increased risk of type 2 diabetes, so advise lifestyle change and glucose checks
why_correct: PMOS (formerly PCOS) is associated with insulin resistance, which is worsened by excess weight, and carries a long-term risk of impaired glucose tolerance, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Women should be told about these risks, encouraged to adopt healthy lifestyle measures with weight management where appropriate, and have their metabolic risk reviewed periodically. Source: NICE CKS, Polycystic ovary syndrome, Last revised in March 2025.
why_wrong: A. PMOS is not a cause of early menopause, and bone density is not routinely monitored. C. Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and is not linked to insulin resistance in PMOS. D. Ovarian cancer risk is not raised enough to justify CA-125 screening, although endometrial cancer risk is increased with prolonged amenorrhoea. E. Long-term metabolic and cardiovascular risks are higher than average, so follow-up is needed.
pearl: PMOS raises the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, so counsel and review accordingly.
thinking: PMOS with obesity and acanthosis nigricans  ↓  Insulin resistance is the driver  ↓  Long-term type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk  ↓  Lifestyle and weight advice with periodic glucose review  ↓  Counsel on type 2 diabetes risk and check glucose periodically
exam_trap: C, type 1 diabetes, tempts because both are diabetes, but PMOS acts through insulin resistance, which leads to type 2 disease.
takeaway: Counsel women with PMOS about type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular risk and review them periodically.
notes: Re-angled from a recall item (which condition) to an advice/monitoring decision. No testing interval or numeric threshold keyed. Live PMOS items (END033, OG030, DS141, DS142) cover diagnosis and amenorrhoea, not long-term metabolic risk. CKS summary, complications and management-adults pages opened; all show Last revised in March 2025. The CA-125 and early-menopause distractor rebuttals are standard teaching, not read from CKS.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman who is in the second trimester of her first pregnancy attends her antenatal appointment in October. She is otherwise well and has no long-term conditions. The midwife offers the seasonal flu vaccine, but she says a friend warned her that the injection could give her flu and harm the baby, so she would rather wait until after the birth.

Which is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Wait until the third trimester, because earlier vaccination is not considered safe for the baby
options.B: Have the vaccine only if she develops a long-term health condition during the pregnancy
options.C: Have the inactivated vaccine now, as it protects her and gives her baby early protection
options.D: Avoid all vaccines until after delivery, because vaccination in pregnancy is unsafe
options.E: Have the live nasal spray instead, because it is gentler on the developing baby

correct_answer: C. Have the inactivated vaccine now, as it protects her and gives her baby early protection
why_correct: The injected flu vaccine used in the UK contains no live virus, so it cannot cause flu, and it is safe at any stage of pregnancy. Pregnancy raises the risk of serious complications from flu, and vaccination also protects the baby during the first months of life. Pregnant women are therefore offered it each season. Source: NHS.uk, Flu vaccine in pregnancy and who can have the flu vaccine, 2026 to 2027 season.
why_wrong: A. It is safe in any trimester, so waiting for the third trimester leaves her unprotected for longer. B. Pregnancy itself is an eligibility reason, so no other condition is needed. D. Inactivated flu vaccine is recommended in pregnancy, and not all vaccines are avoided. E. The nasal spray contains live attenuated virus and is not used in pregnancy.
pearl: Pregnant women are offered inactivated flu vaccine at any stage of pregnancy, which also protects the newborn.
thinking: Pregnant woman declining flu vaccine over safety fears  ↓  Injected vaccine has no live virus  ↓  Pregnancy raises complication risk from flu  ↓  Safe at any stage and protects the baby  ↓  Offer the inactivated vaccine now
exam_trap: E, the live nasal spray, tempts as a gentler option, but live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy and the injected vaccine is the one used.
takeaway: Seasonal flu vaccination is recommended in pregnancy, whatever the stage.
notes: Source key sound. Reworded so the key is not 'recommended in pregnancy' restated; stem has a safety-concern angle and a distractor (live nasal spray) that tests the live/inactivated distinction (the live-spray exclusion in pregnancy is standard UK teaching, not stated on the fetched NHS page). No live pregnancy-flu question found (searched pregnan* with vaccin/influenza/flu: only MMR/rubella items). NHS page says safe at any stage of pregnancy and cannot give flu. The Green Book chapter 19 page was opened but only the NHS page was relied on.

stem:
A 46-year-old woman has had six months of progressively heavier periods with spotting between them. Her pregnancy test is negative, her cervical screening is up to date and normal, and abdominal and pelvic examination are normal. She mentions she has been wondering whether this is the start of the menopause.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe tranexamic acid during menses and review her in three months
options.B: Start the combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate her cycle without further tests
options.C: Reassure her that this is typical of the perimenopause and review if it persists for six months
options.D: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine system straight away without assessing the uterine cavity
options.E: Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity

correct_answer: E. Refer for outpatient hysteroscopy to assess the uterine cavity
why_correct: Persistent bleeding between periods alongside heavy periods suggests possible structural or endometrial pathology, such as a polyp, fibroid or hyperplasia, so the cause should be investigated rather than treated empirically. Hysteroscopy allows direct inspection of the uterine cavity and biopsy when needed. Source: NICE NG88, Heavy menstrual bleeding: assessment and management, 2018 (page last updated July 2026).
why_wrong: A. Tranexamic acid treats heavy bleeding but does not exclude a cavity abnormality causing the intermenstrual bleeding. B. Hormonal cycle control without investigation could mask structural or endometrial pathology. C. Attributing persistent intermenstrual bleeding to perimenopause delays diagnosis. D. A levonorgestrel intrauterine system is a first-line treatment for heavy bleeding but only after the cavity has been assessed when there are features of pathology.
pearl: Persistent intermenstrual bleeding with heavy periods warrants hysteroscopic assessment before empirical hormonal treatment.
thinking: 46-year-old with heavy periods and intermenstrual bleeding  ↓  Pregnancy excluded, cervix screened  ↓  Possible polyp, fibroid or endometrial pathology  ↓  Assess the cavity, not treat blindly  ↓  Outpatient hysteroscopy
exam_trap: D, inserting the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, tempts because it is first-line for heavy bleeding, but with persistent intermenstrual bleeding the cavity needs assessment first.
takeaway: New intermenstrual bleeding with heavy periods needs investigation, not empirical treatment or reassurance.
notes: Source key ('investigate') made concrete using NG88 1.3.4 (offer outpatient hysteroscopy if persistent intermenstrual bleeding or risk factors) and 1.3.10. No age cut-off, thickness measurement or day count keyed (the stem age and six months are context only). Live HMB items (BX463, DR104, PAQ894, PAQ16196) cover FBC, LNG-IUS for simple HMB and polyp diagnosis, not the investigate-first decision. NG88 page shows Last updated 07 July 2026; recommendations cited are marked [2007, amended 2018] and [2018], so the year cited is 2018.

stem:
A 31-year-old woman underwent egg collection for IVF five days ago after a long course of gonadotrophin injections, and an embryo was transferred. She now has increasing abdominal bloating and nausea, is passing much less urine than usual, and feels mildly breathless when lying flat. She is afebrile. The abdomen is distended and mildly tender with shifting dullness, and she has no localised guarding. Ultrasound shows both ovaries enlarged with free fluid in the abdomen, and her haematocrit is raised.

Which diagnosis best explains this presentation?

options.D: Acute pelvic inflammatory disease after egg collection

why_correct: Excessive ovarian response to stimulation causes enlarged ovaries and a shift of fluid out of the circulation, producing ascites, haemoconcentration, reduced urine output and breathlessness. The timing after stimulated treatment and the bilateral findings point to ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome rather than a surgical or infective cause. Mild cases settle with supportive care, but severe cases need admission for fluid balance and thromboprophylaxis. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 5, The Management of Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome, 2026 (page last reviewed April 2026).
why_wrong: B. Torsion causes sudden severe unilateral pain with vomiting, not bilateral enlargement with ascites and a rising haematocrit. C. Heterotopic pregnancy would give sharp unilateral pain and haemodynamic collapse from blood loss rather than haemoconcentration. D. Pelvic inflammatory disease would cause fever, discharge and cervical motion tenderness, with no fluid shift. E. Malignancy does not appear within days of ovarian stimulation and would not usually cause a raised haematocrit.
pearl: Think of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome whenever bloating, ascites and falling urine output follow fertility drug treatment.
thinking: Recent ovarian stimulation for IVF  ↓  Bloating, ascites, reduced urine output, breathlessness  ↓  Bilateral enlarged ovaries and raised haematocrit  ↓  Fluid shift from excess ovarian response  ↓  Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
exam_trap: B, torsion of an enlarged ovary, tempts because enlarged stimulated ovaries do twist, but torsion gives sudden one-sided pain rather than a bilateral picture with fluid shift.
takeaway: Abdominal distension with falling urine output after fertility treatment suggests ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome.
notes: Re-angled from the bare recall item into a vignette with the discriminating features (haemoconcentration, ascites, oliguria). Source key (OHSS) confirmed sound. No live OHSS question in plab1-questions.js (searched OHSS / ovarian hyperstimulation). Key is the shortest option. The NHS IVF risks page also lists OHSS symptoms needing urgent care. RCOG page text confirms OHSS is a complication of stimulation, self-limiting in most, severe cases needing inpatient care; the thromboprophylaxis statement is standard teaching not read from the fetched summary page.

stem:
A 33-year-old woman at 35 weeks of pregnancy is brought to the maternity unit by ambulance after sudden constant severe abdominal pain with dark vaginal bleeding. She is pale and sweating, with a pulse of 128/min and blood pressure of 84/50 mmHg. The uterus feels tense and tender. The midwife asks for guidance on the first priority.

What should be done first?

options.A: Start continuous cardiotocography and decide on delivery from the fetal heart trace
options.B: Perform a digital vaginal examination to check cervical dilatation and exclude placenta praevia
options.C: Immediate maternal resuscitation with IV access, fluids and a call for senior help
options.D: Give intramuscular analgesia and observe on the labour ward until the bleeding settles
options.E: Arrange a transabdominal ultrasound scan to confirm the cause before other treatment

correct_answer: C. Immediate maternal resuscitation with IV access, fluids and a call for senior help
why_correct: Severe antepartum bleeding with signs of shock is an obstetric emergency, and the mother is the priority. She should be resuscitated and stabilised, with a multidisciplinary team called, before the fetal condition is assessed or delivery is planned. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 63, Antepartum haemorrhage, 2011.
why_wrong: A. CTG is done once the mother is being resuscitated, and it should not delay maternal stabilisation. B. A digital vaginal examination should not be done until placenta praevia is excluded, and it does not treat shock. D. Analgesia and observation would delay recognition and treatment of a life-threatening bleed. E. Ultrasound can follow once she is being resuscitated, and should not delay it.
pearl: In massive antepartum haemorrhage, stabilise the mother before the fetus is assessed.
thinking: Pregnant with heavy pain and bleeding  ↓  Shocked: tachycardic and hypotensive  ↓  Maternal life first  ↓  Resuscitate and call senior help  ↓  Immediate maternal resuscitation
exam_trap: A, starting CTG first, tempts because the fetus is also at risk, but the mother must be stabilised first.
takeaway: Resuscitate the mother first in any pregnant woman with haemorrhage and shock.
notes: Source key (ABCDE and resuscitation) retained; vignette set as probable abruption so the key is not the diagnosis. Live items OG009/OG044/DR039 ask diagnosis or stable abruption; none keys the maternal resuscitation priority in APH (OG043 is ectopic). The RCOG guideline text (opened as PDF) states: resuscitation started immediately and the mother is the priority, stabilised prior to establishing fetal condition. The guideline is a 2011 first edition; the principle is unchanged, but a reviewer may wish to confirm whether a newer edition exists.

presentation: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy
stem:
A 24-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant attends her GP with two days of stinging when she passes urine and a need to go every hour or so. She has no temperature, loin pain or vaginal discharge and is otherwise well.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Advise a high fluid intake and review only if symptoms last beyond one week
options.B: Send a urine culture but withhold antibiotics until the result is available
options.C: Give a urinary alkalinising agent and repeat the dipstick in a week
options.D: Issue a back-up antibiotic prescription to use only if symptoms worsen
options.E: Send a midstream urine culture and start a suitable antibiotic now

correct_answer: E. Send a midstream urine culture and start a suitable antibiotic now
why_correct: Lower urinary tract infection in pregnancy carries a higher risk of progressing to pyelonephritis, so NICE advises an immediate antibiotic prescription rather than waiting or watchful self-care. A midstream urine sample should be sent for culture before the first dose so that the antibiotic can be reviewed against the sensitivities. Source: NICE NG109, Urinary tract infection (lower): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Fluids alone are not enough in pregnancy, where untreated infection can ascend to the kidneys. B. Waiting for the culture leaves her untreated; treatment starts at once and is reviewed when results return. C. Alkalinising agents do not treat the infection and a delayed dipstick adds nothing. D. Back-up prescriptions are used for non-pregnant women; pregnant women should receive an immediate prescription.
pearl: In pregnancy, treat a lower urinary tract infection straight away and send the urine for culture first.
thinking: Pregnant woman with urinary symptoms and no systemic features  ↓  Pregnancy raises the risk of ascending infection  ↓  Immediate antibiotic, not back-up or watchful waiting  ↓  Midstream urine for culture before the first dose, then review against sensitivities
exam_trap: Choosing a back-up prescription or waiting for culture, which suits non-pregnant women or other situations but not pregnancy.
takeaway: A pregnant woman with a lower urinary tract infection needs a culture sample and an antibiotic started immediately.
notes: Re-angled from a vague 'general approach' item to a concrete management choice. Distinct from live PAQ14935 (asymptomatic bacteriuria found at booking) and NEP014/ID054 (pyelonephritis in non-pregnant women). Antibiotic named by class only ('suitable'), no drug/dose recall. Within-batch: PAN259 skipped as repeat of this learning point.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman finds a smooth, non-tender swelling about the size of a grape at the lower part of one side of her vaginal entrance. She first noticed it a month ago and it makes cycling slightly uncomfortable. She is afebrile, there is no discharge, and the overlying skin looks normal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Epidermal inclusion cyst of the labium

why_correct: A Bartholin cyst is a soft lump on one side near the opening of the vagina, typically at the lower (posterior) part, arising when a gland duct becomes blocked. It is often painless and only becomes tender, hot and red if it turns into an abscess. Source: NHS, Bartholin's cyst (page last reviewed April 2025).
why_wrong: A. A Skene duct cyst lies beside the urethral opening at the front, not at the lower side of the entrance. B. A Gartner duct cyst arises from the lateral vaginal wall, higher up inside the vagina. D. An epidermal inclusion cyst is small and superficial in the skin of the labium. E. A lipoma is a soft, doughy fatty lump and does not follow a gland position.
pearl: The position of a vaginal-entrance cyst points to its origin, and the lower side is the Bartholin gland.
thinking: Painless, non-tender swelling at the vaginal entrance  ↓  Locate it on the vulva: lower side, not beside the urethra and not inside the vagina  ↓  Bartholin gland duct blockage  ↓  Check for signs of infection to exclude an abscess
exam_trap: Confusing a cyst of the Bartholin gland with a Skene or Gartner duct cyst, or calling every vulval lump a malignancy.
takeaway: A painless swelling at the lower side of the vaginal entrance is a Bartholin cyst until proved otherwise.
notes: Source stem was a bare location-to-diagnosis recall; rebuilt as a vignette with plausible vulval and vaginal cyst distractors. Live PAQ16586 is the infected Bartholin abscess (management angle), so not a repeat. NICE CKS Bartholin topic returned 404 on three URLs, so the NHS.uk page was used. Reviewer: the vignette has no red-flag features, so a persistent or atypical lump in an older woman is not tested.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman has had three months of increasing abdominal bloating and early satiety. She has a distended abdomen with shifting dullness and a firm pelvic mass. Liver function tests and serum albumin are normal, and an echocardiogram shows no cardiac cause for fluid retention. Ultrasound shows a complex solid and cystic adnexal mass with free fluid in the abdomen.

Which mechanism best explains the free fluid?

options.A: Peritoneal tumour deposits increasing fluid leak and blocking lymphatic drainage
options.B: Raised portal venous pressure caused by underlying fibrosis of the liver
options.C: Heavy loss of albumin through damaged kidney glomeruli, lowering oncotic pressure
options.D: Right-sided heart failure raising systemic venous pressure and fluid transudation
options.E: Thrombosis of the hepatic veins obstructing venous outflow from the liver

correct_answer: A. Peritoneal tumour deposits increasing fluid leak and blocking lymphatic drainage
why_correct: Ovarian cancer spreads within the peritoneal cavity, and tumour deposits on the peritoneal surface increase capillary permeability and obstruct the lymphatics that normally drain fluid, producing malignant ascites. Normal liver tests, normal albumin and a normal echocardiogram argue against the common non-malignant causes. Ascites with a pelvic mass should prompt a suspected cancer pathway referral to gynaecological oncology. Source: NICE CKS, Ovarian cancer (last revised in May 2026).
why_wrong: B. Portal hypertension needs chronic liver disease, and her liver function is normal. C. Nephrotic-range protein loss would show hypoalbuminaemia and oedema elsewhere. D. Heart failure is excluded by the normal echocardiogram. E. Hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari) causes tender hepatomegaly and abnormal liver tests.
pearl: In ovarian cancer, ascites usually reflects peritoneal disease rather than liver, heart or kidney failure.
thinking: Pelvic mass plus ascites plus bloating  ↓  Exclude liver, cardiac and renal causes with normal tests  ↓  Peritoneal tumour spread with increased leak and impaired lymph drainage  ↓  Suspected cancer pathway referral
exam_trap: Assuming all ascites is from portal hypertension and overlooking an ovarian primary in a woman with persistent bloating.
takeaway: Ascites with a pelvic mass in a woman should be treated as ovarian cancer until proved otherwise.
notes: Source asked for a mechanism with absurd distractors (corneal infection etc.); rebuilt with credible alternative ascites mechanisms and normal liver/cardiac/albumin findings so the key is not a restatement. CKS confirms ascites and/or a pelvic mass needs a suspected cancer pathway referral; the peritoneal-seeding mechanism itself is standard pathophysiology teaching, not stated on the CKS page. Live ovarian items (PAQ902, PAAKT141, PMG092) test CA125/CT, not mechanism, so no duplicate.

stem:
A 31-year-old teaching assistant who is 16 weeks pregnant is told that a child in her class has been diagnosed with slapped cheek syndrome. She sat beside the child for most of a morning two days before the cheeks became red. She feels well and has no rash, joint pain or fever. She telephones her midwife.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure her that no testing is needed because she has no symptoms
options.B: Offer an urgent termination because of the very high fetal risk
options.C: Give oral aciclovir now as post-exposure prophylaxis
options.D: Arrange parvovirus B19 blood tests through the local virology team
options.E: Advise sick leave until delivery and wait to see whether a rash appears

correct_answer: D. Arrange parvovirus B19 blood tests through the local virology team
why_correct: Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy can cause fetal anaemia, hydrops fetalis and fetal loss, so a pregnant woman with significant contact should be investigated even if she is asymptomatic. Blood is tested as soon as possible after contact, arranged with the local virology service. Source: NICE CKS, Parvovirus B19 infection (last revised in February 2022).
why_wrong: A. Infection can be asymptomatic yet still harm the fetus, so absence of symptoms does not remove the need for testing. B. Most exposed pregnancies are unaffected, and termination is not an initial response. C. Aciclovir has no activity against parvovirus. E. Waiting for a rash delays diagnosis and a rash may never appear.
pearl: Exposure of a pregnant woman to a child with slapped cheek syndrome warrants early serology, not reassurance.
thinking: Pregnant woman with significant contact to a child with a rash  ↓  Fetal risk exists even when she is symptom free  ↓  Check the immune status and recent infection with blood tests  ↓  Arrange tests through virology and avoid contact with other at-risk people
exam_trap: Reassuring an asymptomatic pregnant contact, or choosing an antiviral that does not work against parvovirus.
takeaway: Test a pregnant woman exposed to parvovirus B19 promptly, because infection can be silent and still affect the fetus.
notes: Source item was a tautology ('why is assessment important': because of fetal complications). Re-angled to the real decision, investigating a pregnant contact; no gestation threshold or time-window recall is keyed. Live PAQ995 (school advice, risk to pregnancy), ID039 and DS099 are different decisions. Contact definition and testing steps taken from the CKS exposure section.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman at 31 weeks of pregnancy reports a sudden gush of clear fluid from her vagina an hour ago, and her underwear has stayed damp since. She has no contractions, abdominal pain or bleeding, and the baby is moving normally. Her temperature and pulse are normal. In the maternity assessment unit the midwife suspects that her membranes have ruptured.

Which initial assessment is most appropriate?

options.A: Nitrazine paper testing of the vaginal fluid as the diagnostic test
options.B: Cardiotocography alone to decide whether the liquor has drained
options.C: Transabdominal ultrasound to measure liquor volume as the only test
options.D: Sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid
options.E: Reassurance that it is probably urine, with routine antenatal review

correct_answer: D. Sterile speculum examination to look for pooling of amniotic fluid
why_correct: NICE advises a speculum examination in any woman reporting symptoms suggestive of preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, looking for pooling of amniotic fluid. If pooling is seen, no further diagnostic test is needed and care for confirmed rupture, including erythromycin prophylaxis and corticosteroids, is offered. Source: NICE NG25, Preterm labour and birth, 2015 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. NICE says not to use nitrazine to diagnose membrane rupture because it gives unreliable results. B. A cardiotocograph assesses fetal wellbeing and cannot show whether the membranes have ruptured. C. A reduced liquor volume is not diagnostic and a normal scan does not exclude rupture. E. Dismissing leakage as urine without examination risks missing infection and the chance to start treatment.
pearl: Suspected preterm membrane rupture is confirmed by looking for pooling on speculum examination, not by nitrazine.
thinking: Gush of fluid before 37 weeks with no labour  ↓  Suspect preterm prelabour rupture of membranes  ↓  Speculum examination to look for pooling  ↓  If pooled, treat as ruptured: erythromycin and steroids; if not, use a vaginal fluid biomarker test
exam_trap: Using nitrazine paper or an ultrasound alone to confirm or exclude rupture.
takeaway: Examine with a sterile speculum first when preterm membrane rupture is suspected.
notes: Source was a naming/definition recall (leakage before labour and before 37 weeks = PPROM); that is a bare definition, so re-angled to the initial assessment principle, which is the same condition with a real decision. Live DF055 tests infection assessment in established PPROM and BX253 tests term PROM naming, so not a repeat. Gestation 31 weeks is context only; no gestation cut-off is keyed. I did not cite RCOG GTG 73 (page 404), so no claim about digital examination is made.
